title: Why some city birds sing earlier
paragraphs: A. A person living near a busy street might hear birdsong before hearing a single bus. For some species, starting to sing early could reduce competition with the roar of morning traffic. However, sound is only one possible influence. Artificial lighting and warmer overnight temperatures are also associated with urban areas, so a comparison between a city park and a rural meadow cannot isolate the role of noise.

B. A group of researchers studied twelve sites along a railway line that was closed on Sundays for maintenance. On weekdays, the first train passed over the line before dawn. The team put audio recorders in the same trees throughout the study and measured the first song of a common urban species. They also recorded local weather and the onset of natural daylight. A traffic count was not practicable at each site, so the locations were selected to avoid busy roads.

C. At sites nearest the railway, the birds began singing earlier on weekdays than on Sundays. At sites farther away, the weekday and Sunday records were more similar. The researchers considered the possibility that a train might simply mask the first few minutes of song. If that happened, the recorder would make birds appear to start later on weekdays. The observed pattern ran in the opposite direction.

D. The findings do not establish that the birds anticipate a named day of the week. For example, repeated noises before the first train could act as cues. The study also involved only one species. A useful next step would be to repeat the same monitoring for birds whose calls occupy different frequency ranges, because the ability to hear a signal through railway noise depends partly on its pitch.
